name: Azelaic acid
lead: Azelaic acid (nonanedioic acid) is a nine-carbon saturated dicarboxylic acid found naturally in grains such as wheat, rye and barley and produced on human skin by the yeast Malassezia furfur. Industrially it is made by ozonolysis of oleic acid and is used in polymers, plasticizers and lubricants, as well as in some hair and skin conditioners.[1]

In dermatology it is applied topically for acne vulgaris, papulopustular rosacea and pigmentation disorders such as melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Prescription products typically contain 15 to 20 percent, and lower-strength cosmetic versions are sold over the counter in some markets.[1][8] A US prescription gel (15 percent) is labelled for the inflammatory papules and pustules of mild to moderate rosacea.[11] A 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for azelaic acid, a weaker grade than the strong recommendations it gives for benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids.[3]

A 2025 Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists listed azelaic acid among 23 ingredients that cosmetic dermatologists frequently recommend, for acne and for dark spots.[5] In online communities it is discussed mainly as a skin-care ingredient for bumps, redness and marks, and, separately, as an ingredient in scalp products that proponents describe as anti-androgenic; the latter use has not been established in published clinical trials.

paras: Azelaic acid is used on the face and sometimes the trunk for inflammatory and comedonal acne, for the papules and pustules of rosacea, and for hyperpigmentation.[1][8] It is often described as an option for people who cannot tolerate retinoids, and reviews of acne in pregnancy list it among topical agents considered for use during pregnancy.[6]

Reviews describe azelaic acid as a first-line topical option alongside retinoids and benzoyl peroxide.[4] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline issues a conditional recommendation for it.[3] According to Wikipedia's summary of the trials, 20 percent azelaic acid applied twice daily for about three months reduced comedones, papules and pustules in moderate acne, and its effect has been compared with that of benzoyl peroxide 5 percent, tretinoin 0.05 percent and erythromycin 2 percent.[1]

Rosacea reviews list azelaic acid, metronidazole and sulfacetamide/sulfur among the mainstay topical treatments.[7] The FDA label for the 15 percent gel limits the indication to inflammatory papules and pustules and notes that efficacy for erythema without papules and pustules has not been evaluated.[11]

Because it inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in melanin production, azelaic acid is used for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[8] A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials has compared azelaic acid with hydroquinone in melasma.[9] A 2024 randomized split-face trial compared a 755-nm picosecond laser plus 20 percent azelaic acid with the acid alone.[12] A broader review of melasma clinical trials is also available.[23]

Evidence is strongest for acne and rosacea, where randomized trials form the basis of regulatory labelling and guideline recommendations.[3][11] The acne guideline's conditional grade reflects its assessment of the certainty of evidence for azelaic acid relative to benzoyl peroxide and retinoids.[3] In the Delphi study, most consensus ingredients, including azelaic acid, were supported by level 1b or 2b evidence, although some rested on expert opinion.[5]

Clinicians and reviews generally describe results as gradual, with improvement assessed over weeks to months.[1][8] For pigmentation, the comparison trials are smaller and more heterogeneous than the acne and rosacea programmes.

Human trials of azelaic acid cover acne, rosacea and pigmentation. Registered trials include a long-term comparison of an azelaic acid cream with adapalene in acne (n=60),[13] phase 3 programmes of 15 percent gel in moderate facial rosacea enrolling over 1,000 participants,[14] a small study of effects on Demodex mite counts in rosacea (n=20),[15] a study of iontophoresis versus cream in melasma (n=70),[16] and a study in acne with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (n=20).[24]

Published work includes the systematic review and meta-analysis comparing azelaic acid with hydroquinone in melasma,[9] a 2024 randomized split-face trial of picosecond laser plus 20 percent azelaic acid versus the acid alone,[12] and the guideline-level evidence summarised above for acne.[3] A phase 1 feasibility study of twice-daily use in breast cancer patients undergoing radiation is registered as recruiting.[25] No clinical trial of azelaic acid for hair loss was identified.

The US label for the 15 percent gel lists burning, stinging or tingling (29 percent), itching (11 percent), scaling or dryness (8 percent) and erythema or irritation (4 percent) as the most common reactions.[11] Irritation usually appears in the first weeks of treatment, and the label advises discontinuation if severe irritation persists.[11]
Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema, facial and eye swelling, difficulty breathing and urticaria, have been reported, and the label advises stopping use if they occur.[11]

The label states that azelaic acid is minimally absorbed after topical use and that maternal use is not expected to cause fetal exposure; embryofetal toxicity in animals occurred only with oral doses many times the maximum human dose.[11] A 2024 review of acne management in pregnancy includes azelaic acid among the topical treatments evaluated.[6]

Reviews describe antibacterial, anti-keratinizing, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-melanogenic activity.[8][10] It is reported to be bacteriostatic against Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis without promoting resistance, to normalize follicular keratinization, and to lower reactive oxygen species and inflammatory cytokines.[1] It is also a competitive inhibitor of tyrosinase.[1][8] The US rosacea label states that the mechanism in rosacea is unknown.[11]

The compound has the formula HOOC(CH2)7COOH. It is found in cereals, is made by Malassezia on skin, and is manufactured industrially from oleic acid.[1] In plants it acts as a mobile signalling molecule that primes systemic acquired resistance to pathogens, which is a separate line of research from its dermatological use.[1]
Wikipedia reports that in 2023 azelaic acid ranked about 309th among medicines prescribed in the United States, with more than 200,000 prescriptions.[1]

Skin-care forums treat azelaic acid as a multi-purpose ingredient for acne, redness and marks. Separate threads on T Nation, mostly from 2005 to 2014, discuss it as a scalp ingredient for hair loss, often in combination with minoxidil, finasteride or ketoconazole shampoo; users describe commercial or compounded mixtures that include it.[17][18][19][20][21][22]
Current research directions include new formulations, combination creams for melasma and uses beyond dermatology; the registered radiation-dermatitis feasibility study is one example.[25]

lore.intro: On skin-care forums azelaic acid is discussed as an acne, redness and dark-mark ingredient; in hair-loss threads on T Nation it appears as an add-on to minoxidil or finasteride regimens.[17][19]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid is a 'DHT inhibitor' that helps hair loss when applied to the scalp
claims.believers: Posters in hair-loss threads describe it as a topical anti-androgen and say it blocks a large share of DHT, listing it in 'maximum' regimens with minoxidil and a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.[2][21][22]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed for this article describe azelaic acid's established dermatological actions as antibacterial, keratinization-normalizing, anti-inflammatory and tyrosinase-inhibiting, and no clinical trials of azelaic acid for hair loss were found.[8][1]

claims.claim: Minoxidil plus azelaic acid scalp mixtures improve hair retention
claims.believers: Users report using commercial or compounded products that combine minoxidil, azelaic acid and sometimes finasteride or retinoic acid, and say they are keeping hair while on them.[17][20][19]
claims.experts: No published trial examined in this article tests such combinations on the scalp; the clinical evidence for azelaic acid concerns acne, rosacea and pigmentation.[3][11]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid treats acne, redness and dark spots with one product
claims.believers: Skin-care enthusiasts value it for covering bumps, redness and post-acne marks and as an alternative when retinoids irritate.
claims.experts: The 2025 Delphi consensus lists it for acne and dark spots, the acne guideline gives a conditional recommendation, and the FDA label covers rosacea papules and pustules but not erythema alone.[5][3][11]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid is a safe alternative to hydroquinone for melasma
claims.believers: Users commonly present it as a gentler option for stubborn pigmentation.
claims.experts: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials has compared the two agents in melasma; trials of azelaic acid in melasma exist but are smaller than its acne and rosacea programmes.[9][23]
